hops.afterHeading: Three things a working synapse does
hops.title: Adult brains still hold silent synapses
hops.text: Postsynaptically silent glutamate synapses carry NMDA receptors but few or no AMPA receptors, so they give no detectable AMPA response near rest. They were long thought scarce in adults. In 2022 an MIT team imaged 2,234 dendritic protrusions on layer 5 pyramidal neurons in adult mouse visual cortex. About 30 percent were thin, headless filopodia, roughly ten times prior reports. The 614 filopodia with bassoon-marked presynaptic contacts showed NMDA subunit GluN1 with little or no AMPA subunit GluA1 labeling. In separate slices, directly applied glutamate evoked NMDA responses after magnesium was removed; pairing glutamate application with postsynaptic spikes made applied glutamate evoke an AMPA response within minutes.

sources.citation: Vardalaki D, Chung K, Harnett MT. Filopodia are a structural substrate for silent synapses in adult neocortex. Nature 612:323-327 (2022)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A small brown mouse sitting beside a modern microscope and a glass slide on a sunlit laboratory bench.
image.caption: Bassoon-marked adult mouse visual-cortex filopodia showed GluN1 with little or no GluA1; after slice pairing, applied glutamate evoked AMPA responses.

hops.afterHeading: The receiving side: a scaffold that holds receptors
hops.title: The inhibitory scaffold that can stand in for a bacterial enzyme
hops.text: Researchers named the scaffold protein gephyrin in 1992, from the Greek word for bridge, and found its transcripts in every rat tissue they examined, not just the brain. An odd spread for a protein proposed to hold glycine receptors at synapses. Six years later, mice lacking gephyrin explained it. Besides failing to cluster glycine receptors in the spinal cord, they lost the activity of molybdenum-dependent enzymes outside the nervous system. Gephyrin also helps build molybdenum cofactor, a metal-containing helper that many molybdenum-dependent enzymes use in bacteria, plants and mammals. Put mammalian gephyrin into cofactor-deficient bacteria or a mutant plant, and it gets cofactor production working again, at least in part.

sources.citation: Prior P et al. Primary structure and alternative splice variants of gephyrin, a putative glycine receptor-tubulin linker protein. Neuron 8:1161-1170 (1992)
Feng G et al. Dual requirement for gephyrin in glycine receptor clustering and molybdoenzyme activity. Science 282:1321-1324 (1998)
Stallmeyer B et al. The neurotransmitter receptor-anchoring protein gephyrin reconstitutes molybdenum cofactor biosynthesis in bacteria, plants, and mammalian cells. PNAS 96:1333-1338 (1999)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A small potted green plant, a glass petri dish, and a silver metallic rock arranged beside a miniature wooden arch bridge on a lab bench.
image.caption: Gephyrin anchors inhibitory receptors and also helps build molybdenum cofactor, a job its relatives do in plants and bacteria.

hops.title: Gabapentin binds a thrombospondin receptor, not GABA receptors
hops.text: Gabapentin, an anti-epileptic and pain drug, is a GABA backbone with a cyclohexyl ring, yet does not act as a conventional GABA receptor agonist. By the late 1990s pharmacologists knew it bound an auxiliary subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels, but not what that binding did. In 2009 researchers showed this subunit, alpha2delta-1, is a neuronal receptor for astrocyte thrombospondin. In a cell assay, gabapentin weakened association with a thrombospondin fragment. In culture, it reduced new marker-defined excitatory contacts induced by thrombospondin or astrocyte-conditioned medium, sparing basal and existing contacts; in neonatal mouse cortex, most of the drop came from half the treated mice. Whether this matters in patients remains unsettled.

sources.citation: Taylor CP. Mechanisms of action of gabapentin. Rev Neurol (Paris) 153 Suppl 1:S39-S45 (1997)
Eroglu C et al. Gabapentin receptor alpha2delta-1 is a neuronal thrombospondin receptor responsible for excitatory CNS synaptogenesis. Cell 139:380-392 (2009)

image.caption: Gabapentin resembles GABA yet does not act as a conventional GABA receptor agonist; it binds alpha2delta-1, a neuronal thrombospondin receptor.

audio.title: Three detours inside a brain synapse
audio.transcript:
Central synapses look tidy in a textbook diagram. The proteins that build them keep turning up in stranger places. Here are three true stories where brain synapses crossed paths with plants, blood platelets and a kidney pill.

First, gephyrin, the scaffold that holds glycine and many GABA A receptors under inhibitory terminals. When scientists described it in nineteen ninety-two, they named it after the Greek word for bridge. Oddly, its transcripts turned up in every rat tissue they tested, not just the nervous system. Six years later, mice lacking gephyrin solved the puzzle: they failed to cluster spinal-cord glycine receptors and lost key molybdenum enzyme activity outside the brain. Gephyrin has a second job. It helps build molybdenum cofactor, a metal-holding helper used by molybdenum-dependent enzymes across bacteria, plants and mammals. In nineteen ninety-nine, researchers put mammalian gephyrin into cofactor-deficient bacteria and a mutant plant, restoring cofactor production, at least in part. Evolution did not invent an inhibitory scaffold from scratch; it gave an old metabolic protein a second shift.

Second, astrocytes and their reputation. In eighteen fifty-six the pathologist Rudolf Virchow coined the word neuroglia, nerve putty, for what he saw as a connective substance holding the real nerve cells in place. More than a century later, astrocytes turned out to build synapses using thrombospondin, a protein first found in blood platelets. In nineteen seventy-eight, researchers isolated a large glycoprotein released by human platelets after thrombin and named it thrombospondin. Decades later, neuroscientists found astrocytes secreting thrombospondins to build new excitatory synapses. The twist came in two thousand nine. Gabapentin, a seizure and pain drug, is built from a GABA backbone with a carbon ring added, yet it does not act as a conventional GABA receptor agonist. Researchers found the neuronal protein gabapentin binds is a thrombospondin receptor. In a cell assay, gabapentin weakened association with a thrombospondin fragment. In culture, gabapentin reduced new marker-defined excitatory contacts induced by thrombospondin or astrocyte-conditioned medium while sparing basal and existing contacts; in neonatal mouse cortex, most of the drop came from half the treated mice. Whether this matters in patients remains unsettled.

Third, a finished inhibitory synapse does not always work as a simple brake. Phenobarbital, a longtime first-line medicine for newborn seizures, holds GABA A chloride channels open longer. Yet in a nineteen ninety-nine clinical trial, phenobarbital alone controlled seizures in only forty-three percent of the newborns who received it. Rodent work offers one lead. In many immature rodent neurons, N K C C one brings chloride in while K C C two, which takes chloride out, is still scarce. Opening GABA A channels can then depolarize the cell, and whether GABA dampens or promotes firing depends on the brain region and stage of development. In two thousand five, scientists gave newborn rats a surprising helper: bumetanide, an ordinary kidney water pill that blocks N K C C one. The drug shifted the chloride balance in immature neurons, and in a separate test it reduced seizure activity on brain recordings from newborn rats. Testing that idea in newborn babies has taken great care. An early European trial stopped over hearing-loss concerns and little sign of benefit, while a two thousand twenty-one controlled pilot found no significant group difference in unadjusted seizure reduction and saw a possible benefit only in a follow-up analysis where the estimated effect varied with total seizure burden. Extra urination was more common with bumetanide, hearing impairment occurred in two treated infants who also received gentamicin, and the pilot was too small to tell whether bumetanide contributed or to prove seizure benefit without a larger trial. One ion gradient can change what an inhibitory synapse does.
